labels.label: agents running most of the day

electricity.source: US EIA average residential retail price, ~17 cents/kWh in 2025. TODO: confirm the latest monthly figure at eia.gov/electricity/monthly and update.

cloud.note: Typical hosted decode speed for mid-size open models on OpenRouter. Editable; it only affects the time-cost comparison, not the money.

estimate.note: When no measurement exists, tokens/sec is estimated as memory_bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token × an efficiency factor. Dense: 0.75, calibrated on measured pairs in throughput.json (Qwen3 32B Q4 reaches 82% of the ceiling on M3 Ultra and 77% on DGX Spark; Qwen2.5-Coder 32B 80% on M4 Max; small 7-8B models manage 55-60%, so estimates for them run high). MoE: 0.3, because small active-parameter models are limited by routing and kernel overhead rather than bandwidth on Apple Silicon (Qwen3 30B-A3B measures 30% of the ceiling on M4 Max and 23% on M3 Ultra). A hardware entry can override the MoE factor with estimate_efficiency_moe (DGX Spark measures 65%). Measured figures always take precedence and the UI says which you are looking at.

context.note: The context window you want. It sets the KV-cache memory each model needs, and it slows generation down: every token generated has to read the whole cache back.

kv_cache.note: llama.cpp keeps the key-value cache at 16 bits unless you pass --cache-type-k and --cache-type-v. q8_0 stores 32 values in 34 bytes and q4_0 in 18, so the cache shrinks to about a half or about a quarter. Every generated token reads the whole cache, so a smaller one also speeds up long contexts. Both are lossy; 4-bit loses more.

frontier_basis.name: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3
frontier_basis.note: One consistent public aggregate, re-read across every model on 2026-09-11 so the ranking is on a single scale. Hybrid models are shown at their reasoning or highest-effort figure, with the alternative noted per model. Some scores are Artificial Analysis's own estimate rather than a measured run of the full suite; those are marked.
frontier_basis.estimated_note: Marked 'estimated' where Artificial Analysis imputed the score rather than running the full v4.3 suite. 26 of the models here carry that mark.
frontier_basis.band_rule: Each band starts at about 80% of its reference model's score — Haiku-class at 15 (Claude Haiku 4.5 scores 18), Sonnet-class at 30 (Claude Sonnet 5 scores 38) — the same proportions the first version used. The frontier band starts halfway between Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 (51), because the hosted top tier is bunched too tightly for a percentage rule.

frontier_reference_note: Hosted lineups read from the Artificial Analysis leaderboard on 2026-09-11. score_alt is the non-reasoning or lowest-effort figure where the index reports both. GPT-6 Astra arrived on 2026-09-03 and now tops OpenAI's range.

context_decay.why: At batch size 1 decoding is memory-bandwidth bound. Each generated token reads the active weights AND the whole KV cache, so a large context cuts speed roughly in proportion to how much the cache adds to the bytes read.
context_decay.accuracy_note: Within about 20-30% on the three model x hardware pairs where a public benchmark reports both a short and a long context. It is a first-order model, not a measurement; the UI says when a figure has been adjusted.

sorts.label: Cheapest to just use an API

capacity_note: The daily ceiling counts generation only: tokens_per_sec x 86,400 seconds gives the output tokens a machine can produce running flat out, and the total is that grossed up by your input:output ratio. Input tokens are counted in the total but assumed to cost no time, because prompt processing runs roughly 20-100x faster than generation. It is not free though, so the real ceiling is lower than shown - on a heavy input ratio, plausibly 20-30% lower.

api_decline.label: API prices keep falling
api_decline.note: Break-even is otherwise calculated at today's prices, held flat forever. They have not behaved that way: the cost of a given level of capability has fallen steeply and repeatedly since 2023. Switch this on to decay the API price by a set fraction each year. It pushes break-even out, and past the point where the API costs less than your electricity it stops being reachable at all.
api_decline.source: Epoch AI, 'LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly' — 9x to 900x per year depending on the capability level, with a median around 50x over the period studied. A conservative 40%/yr is the default here.
